clue.text: Noise of movement in court's breaking silence

indicators.note: breaking into something means splitting it open, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: SH is the call for silence
to court is to woo; with the 's it gives a plural-looking form

explanation.surface: A sound in a courtroom interrupts the hush as someone moves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'court' reads as a law court but is the verb meaning to woo.
explanation.definitionFit: A rushing sound made by something passing fast, like a racquet or skirt, is exactly this kind of noise.

clue.text: Greatly involved in region's backing for road safety measure

indicators.note: going backwards, so the whole assembled string is read from its end
involved in means set within, so one word sits inside the other

parts.note: parts is a word for a region, as in 'these parts'; the 's supplies the S
deep can mean greatly, as in deep in debt or deeply

explanation.surface: A deeply involved region supports a road scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Greatly' gives DEEP via the adverb sense 'deeply'; 'backing' turns the whole assembly round, not just the region.
explanation.definitionFit: A police device for catching speeding motorists is used to make roads safer.

clue.text: Improper arrests diminished the Met?

indicators.note: both words are cut down, leaving only a run of letters from inside them

explanation.surface: Wrongful arrests have reduced the standing of the Metropolitan Police.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the Met' looks like London's police force but is New York's Metropolitan Opera; the question mark flags the example.
explanation.definitionFit: The Met in New York is a famous house for staged musical drama, so it is an example of this art form.

clue.text: Brave surgeon's imprisoned in Seychelles — that's harsh

indicators.note: being imprisoned in something means being enclosed by it

parts.note: SY is the international vehicle code for the Seychelles
a brave is a Native American warrior, such as a Cree
CH is short for chirurgiae, as in the surgery degree ChB; the 's is read as 'is'

explanation.surface: A courageous doctor is locked up in the Seychelles, which is tough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brave' looks like an adjective but is a noun for a Native American warrior.
explanation.definitionFit: A screeching sound is shrill and grating, so harsh to the ear.

clue.text: Uncovered needle and thread, previously abandoned

indicators.note: coming previously means placed in front of the other piece

parts.note: a strand is a single thread

indicators.note: stripped of its covering layers, leaving only the core of the word

explanation.surface: A needle and thread were left exposed and then dropped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uncovered' strips the needle down to its central pair of letters, ED.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone left stranded has been left behind or deserted, without means of moving on.

clue.text: I'd like to be informed about computers — I know that all too well!

definitions.text: I know that all too well!

parts.note: a request for information, the words 'tell me'
taken as written
IT, information technology, means computers

explanation.surface: Someone asks to learn about computers, then sighs that they already know the pain.
explanation.definitionFit: This idiom is a rueful agreement, meaning you have had the same bad experience yourself.

clue.text: Sportsman, one who settled by river

parts.note: the Angles were a Germanic people who settled in England, so one was an Angle
R is the map abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: An athlete who made his home beside a river.
explanation.definitionFit: Fishing with rod and line is a sport, so one who does it is a sportsman.

clue.text: Programme broadcast to crowd in front of house

indicators.note: placed in front of means this piece comes first
scattered widely, so the letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A show transmitted to a crowd assembled outside a house.
explanation.definitionFit: This long-running BBC science-fiction series is a television programme.

clue.text: Departs with young swimmer right away to search

parts.note: D is the timetable abbreviation for departs

indicators.note: right away means the letter for right is sent away from the word

parts.note: an elver is a young eel

explanation.surface: Someone leaves at once with a young swimmer to hunt for something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'right away' looks like 'immediately' but means remove R.
explanation.definitionFit: To dig into or probe deeply for information is to search thoroughly.

clue.text: Feature intellectual from EastEnders in discussion

indicators.note: spoken the way a Cockney East Londoner talks, dropping the opening H

parts.note: a highbrow is an intellectual

explanation.surface: An item about a brainy character from the BBC soap EastEnders being talked over.
explanation.walkthrough: EastEnders is a BBC soap set in East London, whose Cockney speech drops initial H.
explanation.definitionFit: A facial feature is any part of the face, such as the arch of hair over each eye.

clue.text: Bear with one in hope for improvement

indicators.note: the letters are reworked to make something better

explanation.surface: Put up with someone in the hope they will get better.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bear' looks like the verb 'endure' but is the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: A. A. Milne's honey-loving toy from the Hundred Acre Wood is a famous bear.

clue.text: Joe's in the pub, having good reason

indicators.note: in means placed inside the other piece

parts.note: the local is one's neighbourhood pub
GI Joe is an American soldier, so Joe gives GI; the 's is read as 'is'

explanation.surface: Joe being in the pub has a sound explanation.
explanation.definitionFit: A rational argument or conclusion is one based on sound reasoning.

clue.text: Criminal charge in Delaware leads to hanging

indicators.note: in means placed inside the other piece

parts.note: DE is the postal abbreviation for Delaware
a rap is a criminal charge, as in 'beat the rap'

explanation.surface: A criminal charge in a US state ends with execution.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hanging' suggests execution but means a curtain.
explanation.definitionFit: A curtain or hung length of fabric is a hanging in the sense of a wall or window covering.

clue.text: Wee lassie at the top?

definitions.meaning: a wee is childish slang for urinating, and so is this phrase
one's lass or sweetheart is one's favourite person, the first in one's affections
the leading record in the charts sits at the top

explanation.surface: A little Scottish girl stands at the summit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wee lassie' reads as Scottish for small girl, but splits into three senses of one phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a childish word for urination, a term for a sweetheart, and the chart-topping record.

clue.text: Liberal charity works keeping monarch regularly stressed

indicators.note: keeping means holding something inside
the letters are worked over into a new form

parts.note: HM is short for His or Her Majesty

explanation.surface: A Liberal charity's projects back the King in a regularly emphasised way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'works' rearranges CHARITY into RHYTICA, which holds HM; L for Liberal then goes at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Verse with a beat that recurs at even intervals has its emphasis falling in a regular pattern.

clue.text: Yen to rent house proves practicable, after abandoning Welsh county

indicators.note: to house is to contain, so the first pair of pieces holds the other

parts.note: Y is the symbol for yen, Japan's currency
to hire is to rent

indicators.note: abandoning means leaving the letter behind, so it is dropped

parts.note: a plan that works proves practicable

explanation.surface: Wanting to rent a home turns out feasible after leaving a county in Wales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'house' looks like the thing being rented but is the verb for containing. 'abandoning Welsh' drops W from WORKS; 'after' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the largest county in England, in the north.

clue.text: Small women's group needs money for float

parts.note: WI is the Women's Institute, a British community organisation for women
M stands for money in economics

explanation.surface: A little women's club needs cash for a parade float.
explanation.walkthrough: 'float' reads as a carnival float or cash float but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To be held up in water, like a swimmer drifting along, is to float.

clue.text: One at party making cryptic threat?

parts.note: the answer read as an instruction: the letters of 'hatter' made mad, that is jumbled, give the word threat

explanation.surface: A partygoer issuing a veiled menace.
explanation.walkthrough: The party is the tea party in Alice in Wonderland.
explanation.definitionFit: Lewis Carroll's character hosts the mad tea party with the March Hare, so is one at a party.

clue.text: Urges lecturer to kill, offering kitchen implement

parts.note: to egg on is to urge
ice is slang for kill

explanation.surface: A violent instruction to murder a lecturer, offered with a utensil.
explanation.definitionFit: A flat slotted spatula for lifting fried food out of a pan is a kitchen tool.

clue.text: Time to retire after group's close shave

indicators.note: after means this piece follows the other
the close of a word is its final letter
to retire is to go back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: an era is a period of time

explanation.surface: Time for the band to bow out after a narrow escape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'close shave' looks like a near miss but splits: 'close' is the indicator, 'shave' the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To trim off a thin layer, as with a razor or knife, is to shave something down.

clue.text: Keep long dissertation's opening short somehow

indicators.note: somehow means in some unexplained way, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the word long as written, then the opening letter of the word dissertation

explanation.surface: Keep a long thesis's introduction brief by some means.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keep' looks like a verb but is the noun for a castle's tower. 'opening' takes just the first letter of 'dissertation', which joins the anagram pool.
explanation.definitionFit: A keep is the fortified central tower of a castle, a defensive refuge.

clue.text: Plant is right outside church

indicators.note: outside means wrapped around the other piece

parts.note: a lien is a legal right to hold property against a debt

explanation.surface: A plant is correctly placed outside the church.
explanation.definitionFit: A fungus-alga partnership growing on rocks and walls is loosely classed as a plant.

clue.text: Give poor travel advice: "Motorway goes straight there"

parts.note: M is a motorway, as in the M1
a road that goes straight is straight, so goes stands for is
direct means straight

explanation.surface: Bad directions: the motorway leads right there.
explanation.definitionFit: To send someone the wrong way is to guide them badly on their journey.

clue.text: Money is tight, to a point

parts.note: tight means stingy, mean
S, south, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: Cash is short up to a point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to a point' looks like 'somewhat' but supplies a compass point.
explanation.definitionFit: A person's wealth or income can be described as their resources, as in 'living within your income'.

clue.text: One that returned mimic's pens and ink

indicators.note: pens as a verb means encloses
returned means sent back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: to ape is to mimic; the 's adds S
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Someone who sent back a copycat's pens and ink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pens' looks like writing tools beside ink, but is the verb for enclosing.
explanation.definitionFit: The brown fluid from cuttlefish was used as a drawing ink and pigment.

clue.text: English vice-president rearing grouse

indicators.note: rearing up in a down clue means reading from the bottom upwards

parts.note: veep is American slang for vice-president

explanation.surface: An English vice-president breeding game birds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grouse' looks like the game bird but is a complaint.
explanation.definitionFit: A grouse is a grumble or grievance, a pet irritation.

clue.text: Sound of cold-sufferer, or of what one needs?

indicators.note: or the sound of, carrying on from the first words, so the phrase is as it is said aloud

parts.note: someone with a cold needs a tissue

explanation.surface: A riddle about the noise a cold victim makes.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken with a blocked nose, 'a tissue' sounds like a sneeze.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the British way of writing a sneeze, the classic noise of someone with a cold.

clue.text: Goes round time and time again, getting most worn-out

indicators.note: going round means surrounding the other piece

parts.note: goes are attempts, tries
a second T for time

explanation.surface: Repeating the same circuit over and over leaves one exhausted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goes' looks like a verb but is a plural noun, attempts.
explanation.definitionFit: Trite means stale from overuse, so the superlative is the most hackneyed.

clue.text: Dirk, unasked, ordered sandwiches hot

indicators.note: sandwiches means holds between, so one piece goes inside
put in order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Dirk, without being asked, ordered hot sandwiches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dirk' looks like a man's name but is a dagger. 'ordered' turns UNASKED into SKEANDU, and H goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: The small knife tucked into the sock with Highland dress is a Scottish dagger.

clue.text: The man entering can try again

indicators.note: entering means going inside the other piece

parts.note: can is slang for the backside, the rear
he is the pronoun for a man

explanation.surface: A man walking into a toilet can have another go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'try' is the legal sense: to hear a case in court again.
explanation.definitionFit: To try a case in court a second time is to hear it once more.
